opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. When I started out, much of my work was very systems-oriented. You'd pick a task, like parsing or translation, and the goal was to build something that worked better: better models, better inference, better software. A lot of that came from a structured-prediction background, where you care about the algorithm and you can say precisely what it's doing.

What changed, and I don't think this is unique to me, is that the field moved underneath us. Once you have very large models trained on huge amounts of data, the interesting questions aren't always "can I engineer a cleverer system?" They become "what is this thing actually doing, and why?" Our theory doesn't really predict a lot of the behavior we see. So you end up acting more like a natural scientist: you run careful experiments, you control what you can, you try to isolate a phenomenon, and you're honest about what you don't understand.

I'd describe it less as abandoning building and more as building in service of understanding. I still write a lot of code, and I still think tools and open implementations matter enormously, because they're what let other people reproduce and probe things. But the question now is more often "what experiment would actually change my mind?" than "what's the state of the art on this benchmark?"

Part of it is also humility. I've been surprised enough times by what scale does, or by which simple baselines turn out to be hard to beat, that I've become much more skeptical of my own intuitions. Empiricism is a way of taking that seriously. You let the experiments tell you what's true, and you try to build up a picture piece by piece instead of assuming you already know the shape of the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says very large models shifted attention away from engineering better systems, but it does not identify Transformer and BERT as the catalysts.

r002.rationale: The response describes uncertainty about what large models are doing and why, and says current theory does not predict much of their behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth saying that when I started out, I really did think of myself as someone who builds things. My thesis work was on structured prediction, parsing, things like dual decomposition for inference, and the appeal there was that you had a problem with real structure and you could design an algorithm that respected that structure. There was a kind of elegance to it. You'd write down a model, you'd derive the inference procedure, and the system was in some sense a reflection of your understanding of the problem.

And then, you know, the field changed under all of us. Around 2014, 2015, with sequence-to-sequence and attention, it became pretty clear that a lot of the machinery I'd spent years on was going to be subsumed by much more general architectures trained with a lot of data. I'd love to say I saw that immediately and gracefully adapted, but honestly there was a period of resistance. I remember thinking that these models were sort of cheating, that they weren't really capturing linguistic structure, they were just memorizing. Which, in retrospect, was partly a defense mechanism.

What shifted for me, I think, was a more honest reckoning with what we actually know. The structured approach came with a lot of implicit claims about how language works, and most of those claims were never really tested. They were assumptions baked into the model. Once large neural models started working as well as they did, you had to ask: what did we actually learn from the earlier approach, and what did we just assert? And the uncomfortable answer was that a lot of it was assertion.

So the empiricist turn, for me, is less about abandoning theory and more about treating the model as something to be studied rather than designed. If a transformer learns something that looks like syntax, that's a finding, that's evidence about what's recoverable from text. If it fails on a certain kind of composition, that's also a finding. I became much more interested in running the experiment carefully than in having the right prior going in. And I think that's actually a healthier scientific posture, even if it's less satisfying aesthetically.

The thing I try to hold onto from the earlier era is a sense of what a real explanation looks like. There's a version of empiricism that's just benchmark chasing, and I don't find that very interesting. What I want is to run the experiments that distinguish between hypotheses, to have some clarity about what would surprise me. So I'd say I'm a builder who got humbled into being an experimentalist, but who still cares a lot about the question of why.

r001.rationale: The response says newer neural architectures subsumed much of his earlier machinery, but it does not mention BERT as a cause.

r002.rationale: He describes a reckoning with what researchers actually know, notes that earlier claims were untested, and says this led him to study what models learn through experiments.

astra-6.text:
I think of it less as a clean break and more as a change in where the interesting questions are. When you’re building an NLP system, you have a lot of decisions to make about how to represent the problem and what structure to put into the model. The research is often in those decisions. You have an idea, you build it, and you see whether it works.

As the models have become more general, there’s this other activity that becomes really compelling: you have a system that works surprisingly well, but you don’t have a satisfying account of why it works or where it will fail. So you start designing experiments to distinguish between explanations. What did the model actually learn? Which parts of the training setup matter? Is the improvement coming from the thing you think it’s coming from?

That still feels closely connected to building systems to me. Building gives you intuitions, but you have to be willing to let the experiments tell you those intuitions are wrong. The shift is probably toward spending more time on that process, rather than treating a better benchmark number as the end of the story.

r001.rationale: The response discusses increasingly general models and a shift toward experiments, but it does not mention Transformers or BERT, or say that they made architecture and algorithm work less pressing.

r002.rationale: It says models can work surprisingly well without a satisfying account of why they work or where they fail, and describes designing experiments to investigate that uncertainty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the continuity is that I’ve always liked building things. When you build an NLP system, you have a concrete task, and the question is: can I make this work? But in building it, you run into things you don’t understand. Why does this choice matter so much? Why does something that seems important turn out not to matter at all?

The shift, for me, is toward making those observations the subject of the research. Instead of only trying to improve the system, you try to set up an experiment that tells you something about how it works. And that requires a different kind of discipline, because getting a better number doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve understood anything.

So I don’t see building and empiricism as separate activities. Building gives you contact with the thing you’re studying. The challenge is to turn that experience into a question you can actually test, and to be willing to have the experiment change your mind.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building NLP systems and shifting toward experiments, but does not mention Transformers or BERT making architecture and algorithm work less pressing.

r002.rationale: The response says building systems raised questions about things he did not understand, then describes making experiments to learn how systems work.
